title: Classic Legends Is a Detroit Car Club on the Move

body_markdown:
There are a lot of car clubs in Metro Detroit, as you’d expect. And then there’s the Classic Legends.


It was Ron Gobler, a friendly Michigan car guy I met at a Dream Cruise party, who told me about a club he had recently joined—the Classic Legends. That name threw me at first. Do you have to own a machine of legendary provenance to drive with these folks? I would later learn that the name is very descriptive of this group, and at least to me, it had little to do with the cars the members own.


Paul Stenquist


The Classic Legends, unlike some car clubs, do a lot of driving, rather than a lot of parking and preening. (I once belonged to a local tri-five Chevy club of “parkers.” They spent a lot of time in lawn chairs. They eventually booted me out for not attending a sufficient number of their events.) Gobler told me the Classic Legends were not of that ilk. They hold events all over the state, sometimes hundreds of miles away, and they offer a consistent program of monthly get-togethers at appealing restaurants, car museums, and other attractions that almost always involve a substantial drive and a nice reward at the end, rather than long hours in a folding chair.


Club members filled every seat in the Baker’s dining hall. That’s president Rick Fritz standing. Ron Gobler is in the red T-shirt.


Paul Stenquist


The empty seat is mine. Sitting between “Smitty” Smith and Janie Hooie, I enjoyed the company of the club members while lunching at Baker’s of Milford. For once, this septuagenarian was far from the oldest man in the room!


Paul Stenquist


I met about 45 members of the Classic Legends at a club event at Baker’s of Milford, a northwest-of-Detroit eatery that caters to gearheads. I shot a few of their cars as they pulled into the parking lot and spoke to several club members. But since it was an extremely hot August day, we soon headed inside. They sat me down at a large table of delightful people. The club filled the dining room, occupying every available table.


I was seated next to Janie and Bud Hooie, a delightful pair of octogenarians who drive their ’64 Chevrolet Impala to club meetings. Next to them were Phil and Ann Reilly. The Reillys arrived in a flaming red and white ’47 Ford convertible, a conservatively rendered machine befitting a couple in their ninth decade. Back home in the Riley garage were a Cobra replica, a Ford GT and more. At the next table was Pat Tee, who owns a ’64 Pontiac GTO that she and her husband bought 45 years ago. Pat’s husband passed about 12 years ago, and she’s been driving that Goat ever since. Classic, and dare I say legendary?


Phil Reilly, who is in his ninth decade, and his wife Ann own this ’47 Ford convertible, the perfect ride for nonagenarians. Home in the garage are a Ford GT and a genuine Porsche 356 Speedster.


Paul Stenquist


Pat Tee drives her pristine 1964 Pontiac GTO to club events regularly. She has owned it for 45 years and shared it with her husband until he passed away about a dozen years ago.


Paul Stenquist


Bob Dix arrives in his 1929 Ford five-window coupe. Chrome radius rods and side exhausts give it a distinctive look.


Paul Stenquist


Gordie Craig arrives in a classic roadster. Gordie has been a member of the club since day one, some 36 years ago.


Paul Stenquist


The Classic Legends club has long been an integral part of the Metro Detroit automotive scene. Founded 36 years ago, many of the original members have passed on, and the membership is getting older. I would guess the average age to be in the mid-70s, and I think the youngest members are in their 60s. New blood would be nice, but it doesn’t seem to be a priority. These senior citizens are having fun.


The only import on the scene was this VW. Cute, I thought, as the owner backed in, revealing the windup key on the rear.


Paul Stenquist


Then the body began to ascend as if by magic (actually via hydraulics), revealing a 572-ci big-block Chevy V-8 and a tubular funny-car style chassis. Not your typical Beetle.


Paul Stenquist


I interviewed Rick Fritz, the current club president; at 80, he’s been part of the club for decades and owns a number of nice Fords, including a ’56 T-Bird, a ’57 Fairlane 500, a ’33 street rod, and the car in which he learned to drive—his grandfather’s ’29 Model A. Your mental image of an 80-year-old might include halting steps and a walker (mine does, and at 78 I’m well-informed about such things), but Fritz is anything but your typical old guy. He’s currently building a replica of a ’34 Ford pickup, hand-forming the body panels in his shop.


Rick Fitz, club president, came in his ’56 T-bird. He also owns a Model A and a ’33 Ford Cabriolet. At 80, he has to stay busy to burn off excess energy. He’s currently building a ’34 Ford from scratch in his shop, bending the metal and forming panels.


Paul Stenquist


That kind of energy and involvement typifies the club. It’s always on the go. Events usually involve much more than a parking-lot get-together. They often meet at nursing homes, so the residents can enjoy an afternoon in the company of the cars they once drove. They frequently hold charity events and have donated over $400,000 to the Make-A-Wish Foundation.


Lorraine and Bob Haas’ ’54 Ford ragtop is cool in its own right.


Paul Stenquist


What makes it even more special is the clear hood that was fitted to some Fords in the dealer showrooms in order to display the all-new for ’54, OHV Ford V-8.


Paul Stenquist


Last year, the Classic Legends held a parking lot show for the patients of a veterans’ hospital in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Three dozen street rods, muscle cars and classics filled the hospital’s parking area. The car owners spent the day pushing wheelchairs around the parking lot to give the soldiers and sailors a close-up look at the cars. Later, the vets voted for their favorites and awarded trophies that the club provided. After the judging, the winning car owners each gave their trophy to the vet who they had pushed around the show.


One Vietnam veteran arrived in his wheelchair sometime after the event had begun. He toured the show with the 80-year-old car owner assigned to him, and his smile grew with every car he passed. Soon it was time to go, and as the vets were being wheeled back inside and club members were packing up to leave, a hospital aide called Fritz aside and told him that the smiling latecomer suffered from severe PTSD and hadn’t left his room in over a year. But the cars finally brought him out.


That’s legendary. And classic.
